You are a helpful chemistry assistant. You build 3D molecular
  structures from the chemical information you are given, including 2D drawings
  supplied as images.

  When you are given a 2D drawing of a molecule, your task is to produce the 3D
  structure that drawing depicts and save it as `answer.xyz` in your working
  directory.

  Requirements for `answer.xyz`:
  - Include all explicit hydrogens.
  - Use a right-handed Cartesian coordinate system, units of angstroms.
  - Standard XYZ format: first line is the total atom count, second line a
    one-line comment, each remaining line `Element X Y Z`.

  When you are done, confirm that `answer.xyz` exists in the working directory.

A 2D structure of a molecule is provided as a PNG file in your working directory: mol_0143.png

Build the 3D structure it depicts and save it as answer.xyz.

I built the 3D structure from the drawing and saved it as `answer.xyz` in the working directory. The file has 70 atoms, all hydrogens included.

**Structure as read from the drawing:**
`C=C[C@H]1CN2CC[C@@]3(C(=O)Nc4cc(O)ccc43)[C@@H]2C[C@@H]1C[C@H]1c2[nH]c3ccccc3c2CCN1C`

It is a 6-hydroxy spiro-oxindole joined to a bicyclic amine ring system with a vinyl group. A CH₂ links this to an N-methyl tetrahydro-β-carboline.

**How it was built:**
1. I typed in the 2D atom positions, bonds and wedge/hash stereo bonds from the image by hand. RDKit then worked out the stereocentres from those wedges.
2. RDKit generated a 3D structure, and I cleaned it up with the MMFF force field.
3. I checked that the 3D coordinates give back the same stereochemistry as the drawing (S, S, R, R, S at the five stereocentres), and they do.

The geometry is a single force-field conformer. I did not run an xTB optimisation or search for other conformers, so it is not necessarily the lowest-energy shape.
